name: parallel-hashmap (phmap)
workload: Inserting up to 100 million key/value pairs (two 8-byte integers) into phmap::flat_hash_map vs std::unordered_map, per the project's online design writeup.
claimed_speedup: "the Abseil flat_hash_map is significantly faster that the default stl implementation, typically about three times faster" (phmap::flat_hash_map is a header-only port of Abseil's swiss-table design); phmap::parallel_flat_hash_map is slightly slower than flat_hash_map for small tables, converging above ~80M values.
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 (exact optimization flags not stated)
tradeoffs: flat_hash_map/flat_hash_set move keys and values in memory, so pointers/iterators are invalidated on mutation, unlike std::unordered_map's node-based stability; node_hash_map avoids that at some speed/memory cost; the parallel_* variants add multithreading support and lower peak resize memory at the cost of being slightly slower for small tables. The author now steers new users to the C++20 successor repo 'gtl' (also by greg7mdp, not filed separately here since it shares the same design and no independent benchmark was found for it).
caveats: The '~3x faster' figure is stated on the project's own writeup page without a CPU model, exact compiler flags, or a linked raw-data/benchmark script for that specific number -- only the compiler (VS2017) is named, so this is capped at Tier C rather than A/B.
found_via: gh api repos/greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap (direct lookup); confirmed via https://greg7mdp.github.io/parallel-hashmap/

name: SIGMOD 2025 Contest Solution - Hash Join Pipeline (Robin Hood/Hopscotch/Cuckoo/Unchained)
workload: Hash-join pipeline over the IMDB dataset (SIGMOD 2025 Programming Contest query set), comparing a std::unordered_map-based join baseline against custom open-addressing hash tables (Robin Hood, Hopscotch, Cuckoo) and then a custom 'Unchained' hashtable with columnar late-materialization and parallel build/probe.
claimed_speedup: Baseline (std::unordered_map): ~112s total runtime. Part 1 (custom Robin Hood/Hopscotch/Cuckoo hash tables): ~108s, ~3% faster. Part 2 (Unchained hashtable + column-store/late materialization): ~16s, ~86% reduction vs Part 1. Part 3 (parallel build/probe + slab allocator): ~7s, ~56% reduction vs Part 2. Final: 'Final speedup: ~16x faster than baseline'.
hardware: MacBook Pro, Apple M4 Pro (14 cores), 48GB RAM
tradeoffs: This is a full application pipeline built for one contest workload (column-store, late materialization, custom slab allocator, work-stealing parallel probe), not a drop-in std::unordered_map replacement library -- the individual header files (RobinHoodHash.hpp, HopscotchHash.hpp, CuckooHash.hpp, Unchained.hpp) could be extracted, but only ~3% of the eventual 16x came from swapping the hash table itself; the rest came from column-store layout and parallelism. Single dataset (IMDB) benchmark.
caveats: Coursework project (University of Athens K23a course) by three students, 1 GitHub star, no independent replication. Reporting '16x faster than std::unordered_map' without noting that most of the gain is architectural (not the hash table swap) overstates the hash table's own contribution. libc++ is inferred from the macOS/Clang toolchain, not stated explicitly in the repo.
found_via: gh search repos "hash map faster than std::unordered_map" --sort stars --limit 20

name: Grouped SIMD Hash Table
workload: Single-threaded insert+lookup benchmark with uint64 key/value pairs at up to 2M elements (~80% load factor), including a per-operation (insert / lookup-hit / lookup-miss) breakdown at 1M elements, using SSE2 grouped-metadata probing vs ankerl::unordered_dense's Robin Hood table.
claimed_speedup: At 1M elements: lookup-hit 1.69x faster, lookup-miss 1.21x faster, but insert 0.72x (i.e. ~1.4x slower) than ankerl::unordered_dense. Total wall time roughly ties/edges out ankerl at 1M (71.9ms vs 72.3ms) and 2M (156.3ms vs 157.4ms) elements; ankerl wins clearly at 100k-500k sizes.
tradeoffs: No deletion support, no resizing (fixed capacity, must be pre-sized), SSE2/x86-64 only (no ARM/NEON port), and the insert path is slower than the SOTA baseline it targets -- it only wins on lookup-heavy workloads above ~500k-1M elements.
caveats: Does NOT compare against std::unordered_map at all -- only against martinus/unordered_dense, which is itself already on the KNOWN_LIST as a faster-than-std project, so this is a comparison between two already-fast alternatives, not evidence against the stdlib baseline directly. Result is a narrow/mixed win (loses on inserts, roughly ties on total time). No CPU model stated, capping the tier below A. The README credits an AI 'Deep Research' tool and includes research-log files (INSIGHTS.md, EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md), suggesting an exploratory/automated project rather than a vetted, independently reviewed library; very new (~9 months) and low-adoption (50 stars).
found_via: gh search repos --topic hashmap --sort stars --limit 20, then gh search repos "hash table" "SIMD" --limit 20

name: CYBHash
workload: Mapping Chinese futures/stock/option ticker symbols to values by converting the symbol string into an int64 key at runtime (borrowing ideas from qlibs/mph and MengRao/str) and then doing fast lookup, versus keying a std::unordered_map directly on the symbol.
claimed_speedup: README states 'approximately 10 times faster than std::unordered_map'; the repo's own GitHub description separately states 'approximately 5-30 times faster than std::unordered_map' -- the two first-party figures are inconsistent, and no benchmark script, raw numbers, or workload size is published.
tradeoffs: Only applicable to a narrow, domain-specific key space (Chinese futures/stock/option ticker symbols that can be packed into an int64); it is closer to a specialized key-encoding trick than a general-purpose hash map, and has no license, so the code cannot legally be reused/copied (study-only).
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (all-rights-reserved by default). Speedup claim is inconsistent between the README ('10x') and the repo description ('5-30x'). Zero benchmark methodology, hardware, compiler, or workload size disclosed anywhere in the repo, so the number cannot be independently checked.
found_via: gh search repos "hash map faster than std::unordered_map" --sort stars --limit 20
